course.title: Physics: Motion and Forces
course.description: Move a cart, balance a force and follow the energy. Predict what happens next.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with signed numbers, ratios, basic algebra and square roots. No previous physics course is assumed.

paragraphs: A trolley given a push along a level track slows down and stops, a ball thrown upward rises, pauses and falls back, and a cart that runs into a resting one and locks onto it rolls on more slowly than before. These look like separate facts, and for most of history they were treated as separate, until Isaac Newton showed in his Principia of 1687 that all of them follow from a few laws connecting the forces on an object with the way its velocity changes.

Mechanics is the part of physics built on those laws, and what it gives you is prediction. From where an object starts, how fast it is moving and what forces act on it, you can calculate where it will be a few seconds later, how hard a floor or a cable has to push to hold it still, and how fast it will be going at the bottom of a fall. Some questions are answered more directly by following energy or momentum than by following the forces, and those let you find a car's stopping distance or the speed of two carts after a collision without knowing anything about the brief, large forces of the impact.
outcomes: You'll be able to tell a change in position from the distance travelled, and find an average velocity from a trip or a graph.
You'll be able to predict the velocity and position of an object that speeds up or slows down at a steady rate.
You'll be able to use Newton's laws to find the acceleration that a set of forces produces.
You'll be able to find the work a force does and follow energy between motion, height and heat.
You'll be able to use momentum and impulse to predict the speeds after a collision.

lessons.title: Where did it go?

lead.text: For an object that moves along a straight line, you begin by choosing one point on the line to call zero, which is the **origin**, and one direction along the line to call the **positive direction**. The object's **position** is then the number of metres between it and the origin, written with a plus sign if it lies on the positive side and a minus sign if it lies on the other.

afterFigure.text: The figure sends a trolley from the origin to +5 m in the first case and to −6 m in the second. The plus sign tells you that the first is five metres from the origin in the positive direction, and the minus sign tells you that the second is six metres from it the *other* way. Nothing in the track decides which end is positive, and the choice is yours, but once it is made it has to be **kept for the whole problem**.

lead.text: If the position at the start is the *initial* position and the position at the end is the *final* position, the change is called the **displacement**, and you find it by taking the initial position away from the final one.

afterFigure.text: Because positions carry signs, a displacement carries one too. A trolley that moves from 1 m to 4 m has a displacement of 4 − 1 = +3 m, and one that moves back from 4 m to 1 m has a displacement of 1 − 4 = −3 m, so the size, 3 m, says how far each moved and the sign says whether it moved with the positive direction or **against it**. Physicists write a change in any quantity with the Greek capital delta, so the displacement is written $\Delta x$, where $x$ stands for position.

reveal.text: The dot moves seven metres towards larger positions, which is why the displacement is positive. Switch the figure to the second trip to compare it with a move the other way.

lead.text: Displacement compares only the start and the finish, so it cannot tell you how much ground was covered on the way. A trolley that rolls from 0 m out to 6 m and then back to 2 m has a displacement of 2 − 0 = +2 m.

The quantity that counts the ground covered is the **distance**, which is the total length of the path. You find it by splitting the trip wherever the object turns round and adding the length of each stretch: here the first stretch is 6 m long and the second is 6 − 2 = 4 m long, so the distance is 10 m.

afterFigure.text: A distance can only grow as the object moves, so it is never negative and has no direction, whereas a displacement can be positive, negative or zero. That is also why the runner in the opening, who covered 400 m and finished on the line she started from, has a displacement of **zero**.

cases.label: Out and back: 0 m, 6 m, then 2 m

steps.headline: A trolley goes from 1 m to 5 m and then back to 2 m

lead.text: Both quantities can be found for one trip. **The two ends give the [[displacement|The change in position: final position minus initial position. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]]**, and the turn splits the path into the two stretches that make up the [[distance|The total length of the path, found by adding every stretch. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]].

workedSteps.text: Start with the displacement, which is the final position minus the initial position.
For the distance, split the trip where the trolley turns round. The first stretch runs from 1 m to 5 m.
The second stretch runs back from 5 m to 2 m.
The distance is the sum of the two stretches, so the trip has a displacement of +1 m and a distance of 7 m.

steps.headline: A cart goes from 1 m to 7 m and back to 1 m

lead.text: This time the method is the same, but **the last line is yours to finish**.

workedSteps.text: Split the trip where the cart turns. The first stretch runs from 1 m to 7 m.
The cart comes back to 1 m, so the second stretch covers the same ground in the other direction.
The distance is the total length of the path, so it takes in both stretches.

lead.text: The origin is a matter of convenience. One student puts the zero of a tape at a point on the bench, and another puts hers 10 m further back, so they read different positions for the same trolley.
Whatever amount is added to the starting position is added to the finishing position as well, and so it cancels when one is taken away from the other.

afterFigure.text: The displacement is 6 − 1 = +5 m on the first tape and 16 − 11 = +5 m on the second. A distance is built from displacements of single stretches, so it is unchanged as well, and the general rule is that **positions depend on the origin you chose, while displacements and distances do not**.

reveal.text: The ends alone would have given a displacement of +3 m, so the 13 m is the figure that includes the stretch back.

blocks.text: A standard outdoor running track is 400 m round, and its start line is also its finish line, so a runner who completes one lap has run 400 m and stops on the line she set off from. The 400 m answers one question about her run, **how much ground she covered**, but it does not answer a second one, which is **where she ended up** compared with where she began.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find both the displacement and the distance for a trip along a line, and say why the two can differ.
intro.whyItMatters: Everything later in the course, from speed to energy, starts from describing a change of position exactly.

recap.keyIdea: A position is a signed number from a chosen origin, displacement is final position minus initial position, and distance is the total length of the path.

blocks.text: [[Displacement|The change in position: final position minus initial position. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]] depends only on where a trip *starts* and *finishes*, so it carries a sign for its direction and is unchanged by where you put the origin. [[Distance|The total length of the path, found by adding every stretch. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]] adds every stretch of the path, so a trip that turns round has a **distance greater than the size of its displacement**, and a trip that returns to its start has a displacement of **zero**.

recap.nextHook: Neither quantity says how long a trip took, and dividing by the time is what gives speed and velocity.

lessons.title: Speed and direction

lead.text: Two trolleys each travel 12 m along a track, the first in 3 s and the second in 6 s. The time that passes between the start of a trip and its end is called the **elapsed time**, and the total distance divided by the elapsed time is the **average speed**.

afterFigure.text: The first trolley covers 12 ÷ 3 = 4 m in every second and the second covers 12 ÷ 6 = 2 m in every second. The unit follows from the division, since metres divided by seconds gives *metres per second*, written m/s. The word *average* matters, because a trolley need not move at a steady pace: the figure says only how much ground was covered **over the whole elapsed time**. Only the [[distance|The total length of the path, found by adding every stretch. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]] travelled is used here, and not which way the trolley went.

lead.text: When the direction matters, the displacement takes the place of the distance, and the **average velocity** is the displacement divided by the elapsed time.

afterFigure.text: The unit is m/s again, but because the displacement carries a sign, so does the velocity. The first trolley is displaced +8 m in 2 s, so its average velocity is +8 ÷ 2 = +4 m/s, and the second is displaced −9 m in 3 s, so its average velocity is −9 ÷ 3 = −3 m/s. Their average speeds are 4 m/s and 3 m/s, but only the velocities show, through their signs, that the trolleys **went opposite ways**. The two averages have the same size whenever an object never reverses.

lead.text: A cart rolls 30 m out along a track and then 30 m back to its starting point, taking 10 s each way. Its average speed uses the total [[distance|The total length of the path, found by adding every stretch. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]], 30 + 30 = 60 m, over the elapsed time of 20 s, which is 60 ÷ 20 = 3 m/s.

Its average velocity uses the [[displacement|The change in position: final position minus initial position. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]] over the same 20 s, and since the cart finishes where it began, the displacement is 0 m, so the average velocity is 0 ÷ 20 = 0 m/s.

afterFigure.text: Both calculations divide by the same elapsed time, so the whole difference lies in the top line: the distance counts the trip out *and* the trip back, while the displacement lets the trip back cancel the trip out. A trip can therefore have a large average speed and an average velocity of **zero**, and the average speed can never be smaller than the size of the average velocity.

steps.headline: A trolley rolls 20 m east in 4 s and then 8 m west in 4 s

lead.text: Take east as the positive direction. Both averages are taken over the **whole** trip, so each is found by combining the two stretches first and dividing once at the end, and the [[distance|The total length of the path, found by adding every stretch. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]] and the [[displacement|The change in position: final position minus initial position. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]] are combined in different ways.

workedSteps.text: The elapsed time is the time of both stretches together.
For the average speed, add the lengths of the two stretches to get the distance.
Divide that distance by the elapsed time.
For the average velocity, the westward stretch takes away from the eastward one, which gives the displacement.
Divide the displacement by the same elapsed time.

steps.headline: A cyclist rides 12 m in 2 s and then another 12 m in 6 s

lead.text: The cyclist never reverses, so *only* the average speed is needed, and it is found by **combining the stretches before dividing**.

workedSteps.text: Add the distances of the two stretches.
Add the times of the two stretches.
With the total distance and the total time known, the average speed follows.

reveal.text: Her average velocity over the same 80 s is 0 m/s, because she finishes where she began, even though her average speed is not.

lessons.orientation: Use elapsed time to distinguish average speed from average velocity.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: On 16 August 2009, in Berlin, Usain Bolt ran 100 m in 9.58 s, a world record. Dividing the distance by the time gives a single number for the whole race, but that number describes **no particular moment** of it.
A number of this kind is useful all the same, since it lets you compare one trip with another, and it comes in two forms: one that ignores direction and one that keeps it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find an average speed and an average velocity for the same trip, and say why the two can differ.
intro.whyItMatters: Speed says how quickly ground is covered; velocity also says which way, and every later idea depends on that difference.

recap.keyIdea: Average speed is distance divided by elapsed time, average velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time, and the two differ whenever a trip turns round.

blocks.text: Both averages divide by the same elapsed time, so they differ only in **the top line**: [[distance|The total length of the path, found by adding every stretch. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]] has no direction and adds every stretch, while [[displacement|The change in position: final position minus initial position. Met in 'Where did it go?'.]] keeps its sign and so can cancel. For a trip that never reverses the two have the same size, and for a trip that **returns to its start** the average velocity is zero whatever the average speed.

recap.nextHook: A graph of position against time shows both at once, and the next lesson reads one.

lessons.title: Read a motion graph

lead.text: A **position–time graph** has time along the horizontal axis and position up the vertical axis, so that every point on it answers one question: where was the object at that moment? For an object moving with a steady velocity, equal steps of time carry it through equal steps of position, and so the points lie on a straight line. In the figure the first walker gains 2 m in **every second** and the second gains 3 m in every second, but the second is *steeper*, because it climbs further in the same time.

afterFigure.text: The picture is a picture of the *motion* and not of the path. A line that rises to the right means that the position is increasing as time passes, so the object is moving in the positive direction.

lead.text: The **slope** of a straight line is its rise divided by its run, where the rise is the change in position between two points on the line and the run is the change in time between the same two points. Rise over run is therefore a change in position divided by a change in time, and that is exactly what an [[average velocity|Displacement divided by elapsed time. Met in 'Speed and direction'.]] is.

afterFigure.text: The first line in the figure rises 9 m while 3 s go by, so its slope is 9 ÷ 3 = 3 m/s, and the second rises 3 m in the same 3 s, so its slope is 3 ÷ 3 = 1 m/s. Because each line is straight, *any* two points on it give the same answer, which is why the velocity along it is steady. The sign of the slope gives the direction in the usual way, so that **the slope is the velocity, sign included**, and a steeper line means a greater speed.

lead.text: A flat segment has a rise of zero for any run, so its slope is 0 m/s: the position does not change while time passes, which means the object is *at rest*. A segment that falls to the right has a negative rise, so its slope is negative, and the object is moving towards smaller positions. In the figure a trolley rolls out for 3 s, stops for 2 s and then returns to the start in another 2 s, and read in order its three segments have slopes of (6 − 0) ÷ 3 = +2 m/s, 0 m/s and (0 − 6) ÷ 2 = −3 m/s.

afterFigure.text: A flat line therefore says that the object has **stopped**, and not that it is travelling along level ground, because the vertical axis is position and not height. Switch to the second trip to see the same stop followed by a continuation in the original direction.

steps.headline: A trolley goes from 1 m to 9 m in 4 s, rests until 6 s, then rolls back to 7 m at 10 s

lead.text: Each straight segment of the graph has its own velocity, found from its own two points. The [[average velocity|Displacement divided by elapsed time. Met in 'Speed and direction'.]] of the whole trip is found from only the *first* and *last* points, and everything between them, including the rest, counts as time.

workedSteps.text: The first segment rises from 1 m to 9 m while time runs from 0 s to 4 s.
The second segment runs from 9 m at 4 s to 9 m at 6 s.
The third segment falls from 9 m at 6 s to 7 m at 10 s.
For the whole trip, use the first point and the last point, and the whole 10 s between them.

steps.headline: A trolley rolls from 0 m to 8 m in 2 s, rests until 4 s, then returns to 2 m at 6 s

lead.text: The segments are read as before, and the last line asks for **the average of the whole trip**.

workedSteps.text: The first segment rises 8 m in 2 s.
The last segment falls from 8 m at 4 s to 2 m at 6 s.
The whole trip also has an average velocity of its own.

reveal.text: The 2 s at rest are part of the elapsed time. Leaving them out would treat the trolley as if it had moved for 6 s instead of 8 s, and the average would come out too large.

lessons.orientation: Interpret a position–time graph as changing position, pauses and reversals.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Suppose a walker's position is noted every second: 0 m at 0 s, 2 m at 1 s, 4 m at 2 s and 6 m at 3 s. The list is exact, but the pattern in it, **equal steps in equal times**, is easier to see when each pair of numbers is plotted as a point, with time along the horizontal axis and position up the vertical one, and the points are joined.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a velocity from the slope of a position–time graph and spot a stop or a turn in its shape.
intro.whyItMatters: An average hides pauses and turns, while a graph shows them, so reading graphs is how you read a whole motion at a glance.

recap.keyIdea: On a position–time graph the slope is the velocity, so a rising line is positive, a flat line is rest and a falling line is negative.

blocks.text: Each straight segment of a [[position–time graph|Time along the horizontal axis and position up the vertical axis. Met in 'Read a motion graph'.]] has a velocity equal to its [[slope|Rise divided by run; on a position–time graph it is the velocity. Met in 'Read a motion graph'.]], the change in position divided by the change in time, with the sign showing the direction. The [[average velocity|Displacement divided by elapsed time. Met in 'Speed and direction'.]] of a whole trip uses only its **first and last points** and the whole elapsed time, so a rest or a turn in the middle changes the shape of the graph without changing that calculation.

recap.nextHook: Along each segment here the velocity was steady, and when a line bends the velocity itself is changing, which the next lesson measures.

lessons.title: Changing velocity

lead.text: When a velocity changes, the quantity that describes how fast it changes is called **acceleration**. It is found by taking the initial velocity from the final velocity and dividing the result by the elapsed time.

afterFigure.text: Both objects in the figure gain 9 m/s, but the first does it in 3 s and the second takes 9 s, so the first gains 9 ÷ 3 = 3 m/s in every second and the second gains only 9 ÷ 9 = 1 m/s in every second. The unit follows from the division: a change in velocity in metres per second, divided by a time in seconds, gives *metres per second per second*, which is written **m/s²** and read as metres per second squared.

lead.text: The [[acceleration|The change in velocity divided by the time it took, in m/s². Met in 'Changing velocity'.]] can be negative as well as positive, and its sign comes from the subtraction, so it says which way the velocity is *changing*. An object that slows from 8 m/s to 2 m/s in 3 s has an acceleration of (2 − 8) ÷ 3 = −2 m/s², because the velocity has fallen. An object moving to the left, with a velocity of −1 m/s, that reaches −9 m/s in 4 s has an acceleration of (−9 − (−1)) ÷ 4 = −8 ÷ 4 = −2 m/s², exactly the same number.

afterFigure.text: The two accelerations are equal, yet one object is slowing down and the other is speeding up, so the sign alone does not say which. What does say is the comparison with the velocity: when the velocity and the acceleration have the **same sign** the object speeds up, because the velocity is being pushed further in the direction it already has, and when their signs are **opposite** the object slows down. A negative acceleration is therefore not the same thing as braking, since an object moving to the left with a negative acceleration is going faster and faster.

cases.label: Faster to the left: −1 m/s to −9 m/s

lead.text: An object that holds a velocity of 5 m/s has a velocity change of 0 m/s, so its acceleration is 0 m/s² even though it is moving. Acceleration measures *changes* in velocity and not the velocity itself, and so an object can move quickly with no acceleration, or move slowly with a large one.

A cart pushed up a slope with a velocity of 2 m/s can come to rest for an instant at the top and roll back at −2 m/s four seconds after it started, an acceleration of (−2 − 2) ÷ 4 = −1 m/s² throughout. Its velocity passes through zero half-way, but the acceleration does not stop at that moment, because the velocity is still changing.

cases.label: Up the slope and back: 2 m/s to −2 m/s

steps.headline: A cart's velocity rises from −8 m/s to −2 m/s in 2 s

lead.text: The [[acceleration|The change in velocity divided by the time it took, in m/s². Met in 'Changing velocity'.]] is found in two stages, the change in velocity first and then the division, and **the signs are kept all the way through**.

workedSteps.text: Find the change in velocity by taking the initial velocity from the final velocity.
Divide the change by the time it took.
To check, add 3 m/s for each second that passes, starting from −8 m/s, and the velocity should reach −2 m/s after 2 s.

steps.headline: A trolley's velocity falls from 20 m/s to 4 m/s in 4 s

lead.text: Here the velocity falls, so the first line comes out *negative* and **the sign carries through** to the last.

workedSteps.text: Find the change in velocity by taking the initial velocity from the final velocity.
The velocity changed by that amount over the 4 s.

reveal.text: The velocity changes by 20 m/s towards the negative direction in 2 s. A ball in flight over the Earth's surface gains about 9.8 m/s of downward velocity every second whether it is rising or falling, which the next lessons come back to.

blocks.text: A cyclist who starts from rest and is timed at one-second intervals might read 0 m/s, 2 m/s, 4 m/s and 6 m/s, so that each reading is 2 m/s *higher* than the one before it. Every quantity so far has been an average over a whole trip, whereas this cyclist's velocity is itself changing from one second to the next, and a new measure is needed to say how quickly it changes.

The measure is built in the same way as velocity was: **velocity** shares a change in position out over the time it took, and the new quantity shares **a change in velocity** out over the time it took.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find an acceleration from two velocities and the time between them, and read its sign.
intro.whyItMatters: Forces change velocity rather than cause it, so acceleration is the quantity that the rest of the course explains.

recap.keyIdea: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time it took, and its sign says which way the velocity is changing.

blocks.text: An [[acceleration|The change in velocity divided by the time it took, in m/s². Met in 'Changing velocity'.]] of 3 m/s² means that the velocity grows by 3 m/s each second, and one of −2 m/s² means that it falls by 2 m/s each second. The object **speeds up** when velocity and acceleration have the same sign and slows when they are opposite, and zero acceleration, which is a *steady* velocity, is not the same as zero velocity.

recap.nextHook: A constant acceleration lets you work forwards from a starting velocity, and the next lesson predicts where an object will be.

lessons.title: Predict the next position

lead.text: An acceleration that keeps the same value throughout an interval is called a **constant acceleration**. From the last lesson, the [[acceleration|The change in velocity divided by the time it took, in m/s². Met in 'Changing velocity'.]] is the change in velocity divided by the time, and multiplying both sides by the time shows that **the change in velocity is the acceleration multiplied by the time**. Writing $v_0$ for the initial velocity, $v$ for the velocity after a time $t$, and $a$ for the acceleration, the final velocity is the initial velocity plus that change.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the velocity starts at 1 m/s and gains 3 m/s every second for 2 s, so it reaches 1 + 3 × 2 = 7 m/s. In the second it starts at 9 m/s and loses 2 m/s every second for 3 s, so it reaches 9 + (−2) × 3 = 3 m/s. On a graph of velocity against time both appear as *straight lines*, since the velocity changes by the same amount in each second, and the slope of each line is its acceleration. Any acceleration that is **constant** gives this straight line, and the formula is valid only for such cases.

lead.text: For a steady velocity the displacement is the velocity multiplied by the time, and the same product works when the velocity changes, provided that the velocity used is the [[average velocity|Displacement divided by elapsed time. Met in 'Speed and direction'.]]. A constant acceleration changes the velocity at a steady rate, so the velocity spends as long above the midpoint of its range as below it, and the average is simply the mean of the initial and final velocities. Multiplying by the time then gives the displacement.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the velocity rises from 1 m/s to 1 + 2 × 4 = 9 m/s over 4 s, so the average velocity is (1 + 9) ÷ 2 = 5 m/s and the displacement is 5 × 4 = 20 m. A cart moving at a steady 5 m/s for the same 4 s covers exactly the same 20 m, which is why the second case is drawn beside the first: **the steady velocity that gives the same displacement is the average velocity**.

cases.label: Starts at 1 m/s, a = 2 m/s², 4 s

lead.text: The two results can be joined into one that needs **only the starting values**. Replacing the final velocity in the average by $v_0 + a\,t$ turns $(v_0 + v)/2$ into $v_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}a\,t$, and multiplying by the time gives a displacement of $v_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}a\,t^2$. If the object starts at position $x_0$, its position after a time $t$ is that displacement added to $x_0$.

afterFigure.text: The first term, $v_0 t$, is the displacement that the object would have if its velocity stayed at $v_0$, and the second is the *extra* that the acceleration adds. For an object that starts from rest only the second term remains, so the displacement grows with the **square of the time**: in the figure, 2 s of acceleration at 2 m/s² gives ½ × 2 × 2² = 4 m, and 4 s gives ½ × 2 × 4² = 16 m, which is four times as far for twice the time. Galileo set out this relation in his *Two New Sciences* of 1638, from experiments with balls rolling down sloping planes.

steps.headline: A cart at 2 m/s accelerates at 3 m/s² for 4 s

lead.text: **The final velocity comes first**, because the [[average velocity|Displacement divided by elapsed time. Met in 'Speed and direction'.]] needs it, and the displacement can then be found in *two ways* that should agree.

workedSteps.text: Find the final velocity from the initial velocity and the acceleration.
The average velocity is the mean of the start and the finish.
Multiply the average velocity by the time to find the displacement.
The formula for the position gives the same displacement when it is applied to the starting values alone.

steps.headline: A cart at 14 m/s brakes with an acceleration of −3 m/s² for 4 s

lead.text: A negative acceleration takes velocity *away*, and the formula for the final velocity handles that **without any change**.

workedSteps.text: The acceleration changes the velocity by the same amount in each second, so over the 4 s it changes it by:
The change in velocity is known, and the cart started at 14 m/s.

reveal.text: The acceleration works out as 3 m/s², but it is not needed: from rest the displacement depends on the square of the time, so doubling the time quadruples the distance.

lessons.orientation: Use a constant acceleration to predict velocity and displacement.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A cart rolling at 1 m/s that gains 3 m/s every second is moving at 4 m/s after one second, 7 m/s after two and 10 m/s after three, so its velocity at any later time can be written down in advance, and with a little more work so can its position.

When the velocity is steady the prediction is easy, since the displacement is then **the velocity multiplied by the time**. The harder case is a velocity that *changes* as the object moves, and the rules for it give the velocity and the position at any later time of anything whose acceleration stays constant.

intro.promise: By the end you'll use a starting velocity and a constant acceleration to find a later velocity and how far an object has gone.
intro.whyItMatters: A rule that predicts correctly can be checked against the world, which is what turns the descriptions of motion into physics.

recap.keyIdea: With a constant acceleration, v = v₀ + at gives the later velocity, and x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at² gives the later position.

blocks.text: A [[constant acceleration|An acceleration that keeps the same value throughout the interval. Met in 'Predict the next position'.]] adds the same velocity every second, so the final velocity is the initial velocity plus the acceleration multiplied by the time. The velocity changes at a steady rate, so the [[average velocity|Displacement divided by elapsed time. Met in 'Speed and direction'.]] is the mean of the start and the finish, and multiplying it by the time gives a displacement of **v₀t + ½at²**, which grows with the *square* of the time for an object starting from rest.

recap.nextHook: One constant acceleration is always acting on a falling or thrown object, and the next lesson applies these formulae to it.

lessons.title: Falling and rising

reveal.text: The acceleration is −10 m/s² at the top, just as it is everywhere else in the flight. The velocity is zero there only because it is passing from positive to negative, changing by 10 m/s every second on the way, and an acceleration that were zero at the top would leave the ball hanging in the air.

lead.text: Motion under gravity alone, with air resistance ignored, is called **free fall**, and it covers an object thrown upward as well as one that is dropped, because once the object leaves the hand gravity is the only thing acting on it. The [[constant acceleration|An acceleration that keeps the same value throughout the interval. Met in 'Predict the next position'.]] it gives is written $g$, it points downward, and it has the same value whether the object is rising, falling or momentarily still.

To use the formulas of the last lesson you choose a positive direction, and the usual choice is *upward*. Gravity then gives an acceleration of $-g$, which is −10 m/s² in this course, and the formulas take these forms.

lead.latex: v = v_0 - g\,t \qquad\qquad y = y_0 + v_0\,t - \tfrac{1}{2}\,g\,t^2

afterFigure.text: In the figure the first object starts from rest and the second leaves the ground moving upward at 20 m/s, yet both velocity lines fall by 10 m/s in every second, so the lines are *parallel*. After 4 s the first has a velocity of −40 m/s and the second has a velocity of 20 − 10 × 4 = −20 m/s. The minus signs mean downward, and **a falling object has a negative velocity** when upward is positive.

lead.text: For an object released from rest the first term of the position formula vanishes, and what is left is the amount by which the height drops, $\tfrac{1}{2}\,g\,t^2$. With g = 10 m/s² an object released from rest falls ½ × 10 × 1² = 5 m in the first second, which is the same as 5 times the square of the time, and so it falls 5 × 4² = 80 m in 4 s.

The height at any moment is the starting height with that drop taken away. The stone dropped from 80 m in the figure is on the ground after 4 s, since 80 − 80 = 0, and the stone dropped from 45 m reaches the ground after 3 s, since 45 − 5 × 3² = 0.

afterFigure.text: Because the drop grows with the **square of the time**, a falling object covers more ground in each second than in the one before: 5 m in the first second but 35 m in the fourth, since 80 − 45 = 35.

lead.text: Thrown upward at 20 m/s, a ball has a velocity of 20 − 10 t after t seconds, which is 10 m/s after 1 s, zero after 2 s, −10 m/s after 3 s and −20 m/s after 4 s. The velocity passes through zero at the top of the flight, and the height there is 20 × 2 − ½ × 10 × 2² = 40 − 20 = 20 m.

The flight is **symmetrical**, because gravity takes away upward velocity at the same rate as it later adds downward velocity. After 4 s the height is 20 × 4 − ½ × 10 × 4² = 80 − 80 = 0 m, so the ball is back where it started, and its velocity there is −20 m/s, which is the speed it left with but pointing the other way.

afterFigure.text: A ball thrown at only 10 m/s rises for 1 s to a height of 10 − 5 = 5 m and is back after 2 s, so a throw at **half the speed** rises a quarter as high and takes half as long.

reveal.text: Both balls land together after 3 s. The formulas contain no mass, because a heavier object is pulled harder by gravity but has more mass to move, and the two effects cancel exactly. On 2 August 1971 the Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott, standing on the Moon where there is no air, released a hammer and a feather together and they reached the ground at the same moment. On Earth a feather lags behind a hammer only because of air resistance, which this lesson ignores.

steps.headline: A stone is dropped from 80 m, and we ask for its velocity and height after 3 s

lead.text: Take upward as positive and g = 10 m/s². The stone starts at rest, so each result uses the [[constant acceleration|An acceleration that keeps the same value throughout the interval. Met in 'Predict the next position'.]] of −10 m/s² and **the initial height of 80 m**.

workedSteps.text: The velocity after 3 s is the acceleration multiplied by the time, with the initial velocity zero.
The displacement comes from the acceleration and the time.
The height is the starting height plus that displacement.

steps.headline: A ball is thrown upward at 25 m/s, and we ask for its height after 3 s

lead.text: The ball is already past the top at 3 s, but **one formula still gives the height**, because it works before and after the top alike.

workedSteps.text: The initial velocity alone would carry the ball this far in 3 s.
Gravity takes back this much of that distance.
The height above the start combines the two distances.

reveal.text: Both the initial velocity and the change in velocity point downward, so they are both negative and add together, which is why the stone is moving faster than one dropped from rest.

lessons.orientation: Apply constant downward acceleration to free fall and an upward throw.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The formulas of the last lesson need an acceleration, and the constant acceleration met most often in everyday life is the one that gravity gives. Near the Earth's surface any object that is moving under gravity alone, with air resistance ignored, gains about 9.8 m/s of downward velocity every second, so a stone dropped from rest is moving at **9.8 m/s after 1 s** and at 19.6 m/s after 2 s.
This course rounds 9.8 to **10 m/s²**, which keeps the arithmetic easy and changes a result by only about 2%.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the velocity and height of a dropped or thrown object at any time, and say what its acceleration is at the top.
intro.whyItMatters: Gravity is the constant acceleration you meet most often, and it shows that acceleration and direction of motion are separate things.

recap.keyIdea: In free fall the acceleration is the same downward g, about 10 m/s² in this course, from release to landing, including at the top of a throw.

blocks.text: Taking upward as positive, a [[free fall|Motion under gravity alone, with air resistance ignored. Met in 'Falling and rising'.]] object has $a = -10$ m/s² at every instant, so its velocity is $v_0 - 10t$ and its height is $y_0 + v_0 t - 5t^2$. A falling object has a **negative** velocity, a ball at the top of a throw has *zero velocity but not zero acceleration*, and the mass of the object does not appear anywhere, so objects of different mass fall together when air resistance is ignored.

recap.nextHook: Gravity is a force, and a force is what changes a velocity, so the next lesson asks what happens when several forces act together.

lessons.title: When forces balance

lead.text: Several forces can act on one object at the same time, and what matters for its motion is their combined effect, which is called the **net force**. When the forces all lie along one line, you find it by choosing a positive direction, giving each force a plus sign if it points that way and a minus sign if it points the other way, and adding.

afterFigure.text: With right as the positive direction, the first cart in the figure has a net force of (+15) + (−9) = +6 N, and the second has (+9) + (−13) = −4 N. The vertical forces on each cart, from gravity and the track, are equal and opposite, so only the horizontal ones need adding here.

reveal.text: The cart keeps rolling at 3 m/s, because a velocity changes only when the net force is not zero. Forces that cancel do not bring the cart to rest, and they do not speed it up. The second case in the figure starts from rest, and it stays at rest for the same reason.

lead.text: Forces whose sum is zero are called **balanced forces**, and an object that has no [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]] on it *keeps* its velocity. A cart at rest stays at rest, and a cart already rolling at 5 m/s goes on rolling at 5 m/s along a straight line, with no push needed to keep it going. The statement is called Newton's first law of motion, and he set it out in his *Principia* of 1687, building on Galileo's earlier argument that a ball rolling on a smooth horizontal surface would never slow if nothing opposed it.

afterFigure.text: The idea runs against ordinary experience, in which things that are pushed stop when the push stops, but in those cases a force such as friction is acting against the motion, and so the net force is not zero. Aristotle's physics held that a body keeps moving only while something keeps pushing it, and it took Galileo's reasoning and Newton's law to replace that view with this one: **zero net force means no change in velocity**, not zero velocity.

cases.label: Rolling at 5 m/s, 12 N each way

lead.text: Take right as positive and a cart moving right at 6 m/s. If the net force is +10 N, in the direction of the motion, the cart's velocity grows, and if the net force is −10 N, against the motion, the velocity shrinks, exactly as the sign rule for [[acceleration|The change in velocity divided by the time it took, in m/s². Met in 'Changing velocity'.]] in the earlier lesson said.

The net force therefore says nothing by itself about which way the object is going. It tells you which way the *velocity is being pushed*, and an object can move to the right while the net force on it points to the left, which is what happens to a cart that is braking.

afterFigure.text: In the first case the leftward force of 15 N is greater than the rightward 5 N, so the net force is (+5) + (−15) = −10 N and the cart, still moving right, is being slowed. A **net force does not need to match the direction of motion**, and confusing the two is the commonest mistake in this part of mechanics.

steps.headline: A sled is pulled right with 30 N and 18 N and left with 10 N and 6 N

lead.text: The [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]] is the sum of **all** the forces, each with its sign, so no force is left out and none is counted twice.

workedSteps.text: Take right as positive. The two rightward forces get plus signs.
Enter the two leftward forces as well.
Add all four signed forces together.
The result is positive, so the net force on the sled points to the right.

steps.headline: A crate slides at a steady velocity under 15 N and 9 N to the right and one force to the left

lead.text: A steady velocity means that the forces are balanced, and that fact gives the missing force.

workedSteps.text: A velocity that does not change means that the net force is zero.
Two forces pull the crate to the right, 15 N and 9 N, and one force pulls it to the left.

lead.text: So far the forces have pointed left and right, but the rule does not depend on the direction of the line.

reveal.text: The cables pull up with 11 N + 14 N = 25 N and gravity pulls down with 25 N, so the net force is zero and the lamp stays at rest. A hanging lamp is not free of gravity; it is an example of balanced forces.

lessons.orientation: Add signed forces and distinguish balanced forces from being at rest.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A force is a push or a pull, and its size is measured in newtons, written N. In a tug of war, if one team pulls the rope to the left with 400 N and the other pulls it to the right with 350 N, the knot at the middle responds to neither pull separately. It responds to what remains of the two once they have **partly cancelled**.
Everything so far described how things move; the question now is *why* they move as they do.

intro.promise: By the end you'll add forces with their signs to find the net force, and say what zero net force does and does not mean.
intro.whyItMatters: Forces are what change velocities, so every later prediction starts by adding the forces on an object correctly.

recap.keyIdea: The net force is the signed sum of the forces on an object, and when it is zero the velocity does not change.

blocks.text: To find the [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]], give each force a sign for its direction and add them, so that forces in opposite directions subtract. When the [[balanced forces|Forces whose signed sum, the net force, is zero. Met in 'When forces balance'.]] sum to zero the velocity stays as it is, so an object at rest stays at rest and an object that is moving **keeps moving at the same velocity**, and when the net force is not zero it points the way the velocity is *changing*, which need not be the way the object is moving.

recap.nextHook: A non-zero net force changes the velocity, and the next lesson says by how much, in terms of the mass of the object.

lessons.title: Force, mass and acceleration

lead.text: The same push on a heavier trolley gives a smaller [[acceleration|The change in velocity divided by the time it took, in m/s². Met in 'Changing velocity'.]], and a larger push on the same trolley gives a larger one. The property of an object that decides how much it resists a change in velocity is its **mass**, measured in kilograms (kg), and the relation that links it to the [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]] is called Newton's **second law**.

afterFigure.text: A push of 10 N on 5 kg gives 10 ÷ 5 = 2 m/s², the same push on 10 kg gives 10 ÷ 10 = 1 m/s², and 20 N on 5 kg gives 20 ÷ 5 = 4 m/s². Doubling the mass therefore *halves* the acceleration and doubling the force *doubles* it. The units are chosen so that the law needs no extra constant: **one newton is the net force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s²**, so 1 N = 1 kg·m/s².

lead.text: Because the mass is positive, the acceleration always points the *same way* as the [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]], and it takes its sign from it. The velocity does not enter the law at all. Two carts of 2 kg moving right at 5 m/s, one pushed with 10 N against the motion and one with 10 N along it, have accelerations of −10 ÷ 2 = −5 m/s² and +10 ÷ 2 = +5 m/s², so the first slows and the second speeds up.

afterFigure.text: When there are several forces, the order of working is therefore fixed: **add the forces first**, with their signs, to find the net force, and divide by the mass only after that.

steps.headline: A 5 kg trolley is pushed right with 30 N while 6 N of resistance acts to the left

lead.text: Both forces act on the trolley, so the [[second law|The acceleration of an object is the net force on it divided by its mass. Met in 'Force, mass and acceleration'.]] needs their sum, and then the mass.

workedSteps.text: Add the forces with their signs, taking right as positive.
Divide the net force by the mass.
The result is positive, so the trolley's velocity grows by 4.8 m/s every second.

steps.headline: A 3 kg cart has forces of 18 N to the right and 6 N to the left

lead.text: The steps are the same, and the last one is left to you.

workedSteps.text: Add the forces with their signs.
The net force is known, and the cart has a mass of 3 kg.

lead.text: Multiplying both sides of $a = F_\text{net}/m$ by the mass gives the net force needed to produce a given acceleration, and dividing both sides of that by the acceleration gives the mass.

afterFigure.text: A net force to give a 7 kg object an acceleration of 3 m/s² is 7 × 3 = 21 N, and a net force of 21 N that gives an object an acceleration of 3 m/s² must be acting on a mass of 21 ÷ 3 = 7 kg. The first form also shows why a heavier object needs more force for the same acceleration: **for a fixed acceleration the force is proportional to the mass**.

reveal.text: The net force is the sum of the engine's push forwards and the resistances backwards, so the engine pushes harder than 3000 N whenever there is any air resistance or friction.

lessons.orientation: Use net force and mass to predict how velocity changes.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Anyone who has pushed a loaded trolley knows that the same push that sends an empty one off quickly barely gets a full one moving, and that a harder push on the same trolley makes it speed up faster. The last lesson showed how to find the net force on an object, and what remains is to say *how much* acceleration a given net force produces.
The answer depends on one more property of the object, its **mass**.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the acceleration that a net force gives an object of known mass, and find a force or a mass from the other two quantities.
intro.whyItMatters: One short equation links the forces on an object to how its velocity changes, and the rest of mechanics applies it.

recap.keyIdea: The acceleration of an object is the net force on it divided by its mass, and the law can be rearranged for the force or the mass.

blocks.text: The [[second law|The acceleration of an object is the net force on it divided by its mass. Met in 'Force, mass and acceleration'.]] says $a = F_\text{net}/m$, with the [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]] found first by adding the forces with their signs. The acceleration points the same way as the net force, so **the direction of motion does not matter**, and rearranging gives $F_\text{net} = ma$ and $m = F_\text{net}/a$, so that any one of the three quantities follows from the other two. One newton is the net force that gives 1 kg an acceleration of *1 m/s²*.

recap.nextHook: Gravity is one of the forces that can act on an object, and the next lesson separates its pull, the weight, from the mass.

lessons.title: Weight and support

lead.text: The pull of gravity on an object is called its **weight**, written $W = mg$, and because it is a force it is measured in newtons. Its direction is down, towards the centre of the Earth. The units of $g$ can be given either as 9.8 N for each kilogram or as 9.8 m/s², and these are the same thing, since a net force of 9.8 N on 1 kg gives an acceleration of 9.8 m/s² by the [[second law|The acceleration of an object is the net force on it divided by its mass. Met in 'Force, mass and acceleration'.]].

afterFigure.text: A 5 kg bag has a weight of 5 × 10 = 50 N on the Earth. On the Moon, where $g$ is about 1.6 N for each kilogram, the same bag has a weight of 5 × 1.6 = 8 N, although nothing about the bag has changed and its **mass is still 5 kg**. Mass is how much matter the bag holds and how strongly it resists acceleration, and it goes with the bag wherever it travels, whereas weight is the pull of gravity on it *where it happens to be*.

lead.text: A bag resting on a table has a weight pulling it down, yet it is not accelerating, so by the first law the [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]] on it is zero. Something must therefore push up with a force equal to the weight, and it is the table. The upward force that a surface exerts on an object resting on it is called the **support force**, and it acts at right angles to the surface, which is why it is also called the normal force.

afterFigure.text: The table does not have a fixed push to give: it **adjusts to whatever the load needs**, up to the point where it breaks. The two forces are equal here only because the bag is at rest, and they are separate forces, since the weight is a pull from the Earth and the support force is a push from the table.

lead.text: Put the bag on the floor of a lift that is speeding up as it rises, with upward as positive. The bag must accelerate at the lift's acceleration $a$, so the net force on it is $ma$ upward, and *that net force is the support force minus the weight*.

lead.latex: N - m g = m a \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad N = m\,(g + a)

afterFigure.text: For the 3 kg bag in the figure the weight is 30 N whatever the lift does. At rest the support force is 30 N, and in a lift accelerating upward at 1 m/s² it is 3 × (10 + 1) = 33 N. A bathroom scale in the lift reads the **support force** and not the weight, which is why you feel *heavier* as a lift starts to rise: the floor really is pushing up harder on you, although your weight has not changed.

cases.label: 3 kg bag, lift speeding up at 1

steps.headline: A 5 kg bag on the floor of a lift that accelerates upward at 3 m/s²

lead.text: The [[support force|The upward push of a surface on an object resting on it. Met in 'Weight and support'.]] has to do two jobs, carrying the weight and giving the extra upward force that the acceleration requires, so the two amounts are found separately and added.

workedSteps.text: The weight is mass times g.
The net force needed for the acceleration is mass times acceleration, pointing upward.
The support force is the weight plus that extra force, so it is larger than the weight.
The same result follows from N = m(g + a).

steps.headline: A support accelerates a 4 kg object upward at 2 m/s²

lead.text: The same two amounts are needed again, and the last step is left to you.

workedSteps.text: The weight is mass times g.
The extra net force for the acceleration is mass times acceleration.
The support force has to do both of these jobs.

lead.text: The same equation covers a lift whose acceleration points down, with the acceleration written as a negative number. A 3 kg bag in a lift that is speeding up downward at 1 m/s² has a support force of 3 × (10 − 1) = 27 N, which is less than the 30 N weight, because only part of the weight has to be held up while the rest produces the downward acceleration.
If the lift were falling freely, with an acceleration of −10 m/s², the support force would be 3 × (10 − 10) = 0 N, and the bag would no longer press on the floor at all.

afterFigure.text: In free fall the bag feels **weightless** even though its weight is still 30 N, because nothing is pushing back on it. Gravity has not switched off; the bag and the lift are falling together.

cases.label: 3 kg bag, lift speeding up downward
3 kg bag, lift in free fall

reveal.text: The support force equals the weight. A constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force is zero whichever way the lift is travelling, and only a change in velocity makes the support force differ from the weight.
The table pushes up with only 6.4 N, about a sixth of what the same bag needs on the Earth's surface, although the bag's mass is unchanged.

lessons.orientation: Distinguish mass, gravitational force and the force from a support.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: When a bag is dropped it accelerates downward at g, about 9.8 m/s², and gravity is the only force on it. The second law then fixes the size of that force: the net force is the mass multiplied by the acceleration, so gravity must pull on a bag of mass m with a force of m × g.
Each kilogram is therefore pulled with a force of about 9.8 N, which this course rounds to **10 N for each kilogram**, and the pull on a larger mass is found by multiplying.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the weight of an object, the support force on it at rest and in a lift, and say why weight and mass are different.
intro.whyItMatters: A bathroom scale reads a support force, not a mass or a weight, and knowing the difference explains why a lift can make you feel heavier.

recap.keyIdea: Weight is the pull of gravity, mg, and a support pushes up on what rests on it with a force equal to the weight only when the object is not accelerating.

blocks.text: The [[weight|The force of gravity on an object, W = mg, in newtons. Met in 'Weight and support'.]] of an object is its mass times $g$, so it changes with place while the mass does not, and the [[support force|The upward push of a surface on an object resting on it. Met in 'Weight and support'.]] of a surface on a resting object equals the weight because the [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]] is zero. When the support accelerates the object, the force becomes **m(g + a)**, which is larger than the weight for an upward acceleration, smaller for a downward one and zero in free fall, and a scale reads the *support force* and not the weight.

recap.nextHook: Gravity pulling the bag and the table pushing it are two different forces, and the next lesson asks what each force's partner is.

lessons.title: Forces come in pairs

lead.text: When object A exerts a force on object B, object B exerts a force on A that is equal in size and opposite in direction, and the two exist at the same moment. This is Newton's **third law**, set out in the *Principia* of 1687 in Motte's English translation as "to every action there is always opposed an equal reaction", and the two forces are called an **interaction pair**. The older wording suggests that one force comes first and the other follows, but both arise together and neither has a better claim to be the cause.

afterFigure.text: The two forces of a pair never cancel, because a force can only cancel another that acts on the *same* object, and these act on different ones. The [[second law|The acceleration of an object is the net force on it divided by its mass. Met in 'Force, mass and acceleration'.]] is applied to each object separately, using only the forces on it. In the figure the carts push each other with 8 N, so the 1 kg cart accelerates at 8 ÷ 1 = 8 m/s² and the 4 kg cart at 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s², which is why **equal forces can give unequal accelerations**. For the same reason two forces on one object, such as a bag's weight and the support force of the table, are never an interaction pair, even if they happen to be equal and opposite.

cases.label: A is 1 kg and B is 4 kg
A and B are both 4 kg

steps.headline: A 3 kg cart A pushes a 6 kg cart B with 12 N

lead.text: Each cart gets its own calculation, using the force *on that cart* and that cart's own mass. Take right as positive, with A pushing B to the right.

workedSteps.text: The force on B is A's push, and B's acceleration follows from the second law.
The force on A is B's push back, which has the same size and the opposite sign.
A's acceleration is that force divided by A's mass.

steps.headline: Cart B pushes the 2 kg cart A to the left with 10 N

lead.text: The same method applies to the cart that does the pushing, which feels the pair's other force.

workedSteps.text: Take right as positive. B's push on A points left, so the force on A is negative.
A has a mass of 2 kg, and this is its only horizontal force.

lead.text: It is sometimes useful to treat two objects as a single system and ask about the forces on the whole. If the two carts push only on each other, the force on A is −10 N and the force on B is +10 N, so the [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]] on the pair is (−10) + (+10) = 0 N. The forces of an interaction pair do cancel in this sum, but only because the system was drawn to include *both* objects and the forces are therefore **internal** to it.

afterFigure.text: The cancelling inside the system says that the carts cannot push the pair as a whole in either direction, and it says nothing about the individual carts, each of which still accelerates: the 2 kg cart at 10 ÷ 2 = 5 m/s² to the left and the 5 kg cart at 10 ÷ 5 = 2 m/s² to the right. **Internal forces cannot push a system as a whole**, but they change how its parts move relative to one another, and only forces from outside the system can change the motion of the whole.

reveal.text: The 50 kg skater feels the same 60 N and so accelerates at 60 ÷ 50 = 1.2 m/s² the other way, twice as fast as the 100 kg skater. The forces are equal, and the lighter skater moves away faster.

lessons.orientation: Identify an interaction pair and explain why equal forces can produce different accelerations.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Whenever one object pushes on another, the second pushes back on the first. A hand pressed against a wall feels the wall pressing on the palm, and a swimmer who pushes off the end of a pool is sent backwards by the very wall that she pushed. Forces are therefore never single: they come in twos, **one on each of the two objects that interact**.

That raises an obvious difficulty, since forces that cancel leave an object where it was, and two matching forces ought to cancel and so make motion impossible. The resolution lies in *which object* each force acts on.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name the partner of a force, find the acceleration of each of two interacting objects, and say why their equal forces do not cancel.
intro.whyItMatters: Every force is one half of an interaction, and tracing the other half is how you decide which forces act on the object you are studying.

recap.keyIdea: Forces come in interaction pairs, equal and opposite and acting on different objects, so each object's acceleration is found from the force on it and its own mass.

blocks.text: The [[third law|If A exerts a force on B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. Met in 'Forces come in pairs'.]] says that if A pushes B with a force, B pushes A with the same size of force in the opposite direction, and these two forces make an [[interaction pair|The two forces, one on each object, with which two objects act on each other. Met in 'Forces come in pairs'.]] that **never cancels on a single object**. Equal forces give *unequal* accelerations whenever the masses differ, since each acceleration is the force on that object divided by its own mass, and the pair cancels only in a sum over a system that contains both objects.

recap.nextHook: Contact between surfaces produces another force, friction, which adjusts itself to the push and which the next lesson examines.

lessons.title: Friction that adjusts

lead.text: The friction on an object that is not sliding is called **static friction**, and it acts along the surface, opposite to the push. It takes *whatever* size is needed to keep the object at rest, so that the [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]] stays zero, and so a push of 8 N is met by 8 N of friction and a push of 16 N is met by 16 N.

afterFigure.text: It is a **response** to the push and not a property of the crate: if the push were removed, the static friction would fall to zero, since nothing would then be trying to move the crate. The adjustment has a ceiling, though, because the surfaces can grip each other only so hard, and a push above that ceiling is the one that sets the crate sliding.

lead.text: The ceiling on static friction depends on two things: how hard the surfaces are pressed together, which is measured by the [[support force|The upward push of a surface on an object resting on it. Met in 'Weight and support'.]], and *how well* the two surfaces grip, which is described by a number called the **coefficient of static friction**, written $\mu_s$. On a level floor the support force equals the weight, $mg$, and the greatest static friction is the product.

afterFigure.text: For a 6 kg crate with $\mu_s = 0.4$ the support force is 6 × 10 = 60 N, so the limit is 0.4 × 60 = 24 N. The coefficient belongs to the **pair of surfaces**, such as rubber on concrete or wood on wood, and not to either surface alone. Pressing the surfaces together harder raises the limit in proportion, which is why a heavier crate is harder to start moving.

lead.text: When the push exceeds the limit the object slides, and the friction is now the **sliding friction**, which has a fixed size: the *coefficient of sliding friction*, $\mu_k$, multiplied by the [[support force|The upward push of a surface on an object resting on it. Met in 'Weight and support'.]]. It does not change with the push, and it is usually a little less than the greatest static friction, which is why an object that is hard to start moving is *easier* to keep moving.

afterFigure.text: For a 5 kg crate with $\mu_k = 0.4$ and $\mu_s = 0.5$ the sliding friction is 0.4 × 5 × 10 = 20 N, against a limit of 0.5 × 50 = 25 N for static friction. A push of 30 N on the sliding crate leaves a net force of 30 − 20 = 10 N and an acceleration of 10 ÷ 5 = 2 m/s², while a push of 20 N leaves a net force of **zero**, so the crate slides on at a constant velocity.

steps.headline: A 6 kg crate with μ_s = 0.4 and μ_k = 0.3 is pushed with 20 N, and then with 30 N

The most static friction can give is the static coefficient times that.
A push of 20 N is below 24 N, so the crate stays at rest and the friction is exactly the push.
A push of 30 N is above 24 N, and the friction falls to the sliding value.
The net force is the push minus the sliding friction, and the acceleration follows.

It points against the sliding, which is to the left, so it is negative.
This friction is the only horizontal force, so it is the net force, and the box has a mass of 5 kg.

blocks.text: A crate on a floor does not move when you push it gently, and it still does not move when you push harder, until at some point it suddenly slides. While the crate stays still, something along the floor must be holding it back against your push, and that something is the friction between the crate and the floor.

What is unusual about this force is that it is **not a fixed amount**. It grows as you push harder, up to a limit that depends on how firmly the crate presses on the floor and on the two surfaces, and once the crate slides a sliding friction takes over.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the friction on a box that is held still or sliding, and predict whether a given push will move it.
intro.whyItMatters: Friction decides whether a push moves an object at all, and it is the force that most often needs to be included in a net force.

recap.keyIdea: Static friction matches the push up to μ_s times the support force, and once the object slides the friction is μ_k times the support force.

blocks.text: The [[static friction|The friction on an object that is not sliding; it matches the push up to a maximum. Met in 'Friction that adjusts'.]] on an object at rest adjusts to the push, opposite to it, up to a maximum of $\mu_s N$, and a bigger push sets the object sliding. The [[sliding friction|The friction on an object that is sliding, μ_k times the support force. Met in 'Friction that adjusts'.]] then has the fixed size $\mu_k N$, usually a little smaller, and it **points against the sliding** and enters the [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]] like any other force, so the acceleration is the push minus the friction, divided by the mass.

recap.nextHook: Forces that act over a distance transfer energy, and the next lesson measures that transfer as work.

lessons.title: When a force does work

lead.text: The quantity that combines force and distance is called **work**. When a constant force $F$ acts in the same direction as the object's displacement $d$, the work it does is their product, and the unit is the **joule**, written J, which is the work done by a force of 1 N acting through a displacement of 1 m, so that 1 J = 1 N·m. The unit is named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule, who measured how much heating a given amount of mechanical work produces.

afterFigure.text: A force of 12 N through 3 m does 12 × 3 = 36 J of work, and the same force through 6 m does 12 × 6 = 72 J, **twice as much**. Work is a measure of the energy a force transfers, and it is described as being done *by* a particular force, so that several forces on one object each do their own work.

lead.text: The sign of the work follows the direction of the force relative to the displacement. A force along the displacement does positive work, and a force pointing the opposite way does the same amount of work with a negative sign, $W = -F\,d$. A 5 N force acting against a displacement of 4 m does −5 × 4 = −20 J, while the same force acting along it does +20 J.

afterFigure.text: Positive work adds energy to the object, which tends to speed it up, and negative work takes energy away, which tends to *slow* it down. The [[friction|The force along a surface that opposes sliding. Met in 'Friction that adjusts'.]] on a sliding object is the usual example, since it always points against the sliding and so always does **negative work**.

lead.text: Only the part of a force that points along the displacement can transfer energy. A force at right angles to the motion has no part along it at all, so it does **zero work** whatever its size. The [[support force|The upward push of a surface on an object resting on it. Met in 'Weight and support'.]] of a floor on a crate that is sliding along the floor is at right angles to the crate's displacement, and so is the pull of gravity on it, so neither does any work on the crate as it slides.

afterFigure.text: For a force at an angle in between, only its component along the displacement counts, which is $F\cos\theta$ for an angle $\theta$ between the force and the displacement, and the three cases of this lesson are those with $\theta$ equal to 0°, 180° and 90°. The rule explains why carrying a bag along a level corridor with a vertical lift transfers no energy to it.

lead.text: When several forces act on an object, each one does its own work. The **net work** is the sum of the signed works, and it equals the work of the [[net force|The sum of all the forces on one object, with signs for direction. Met in 'When forces balance'.]], as the earlier rule for adding forces requires.

afterFigure.text: Take a cart that is pulled with 8 N through 5 m while 6 N of friction acts against the motion. The pull does +40 J and the friction does −30 J, so the net work is 40 − 30 = +10 J, and the same result comes from the net force: (8 − 6) × 5 = 10 J. A **positive net work** means that the cart gains energy overall, and a negative one means that it loses some.

workedSteps.text: The pull acts along the displacement, so its work is positive.
The friction acts against the displacement.
The net work is the sum of the two signed works.
The net force method agrees: the net force is 20 − 8 = 12 N along the displacement.

lead.text: The method is the same, and **the last line is yours to finish**.

workedSteps.text: The push acts along the displacement.
The friction acts against the displacement.
Each force now has its own signed work.

reveal.text: Gravity does +100 J on the stone, and the stone gains that much energy in falling. That is the link between work and the motion of falling objects that the next two lessons develop.

lessons.orientation: Calculate signed work for forces along, against and perpendicular to displacement.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A steady push that moves a crate across a floor hands energy to the crate, while a brake pressing against a moving wheel takes energy away. In both cases the amount depends on only two things, how large the force is and how far the object moves while the force acts.

Velocity and acceleration describe a motion moment by moment, whereas a quantity that combines **the force and the distance into one number** can be added up from one force to the next and compared directly with the energy an object gains or loses.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the work done by a force along, against or across a displacement, and add the works of several forces.
intro.whyItMatters: Work is how forces change the energy of things, so it leads from describing motion to following energy.

recap.keyIdea: The work of a constant force is its size times the displacement along it, positive when it acts with the motion, negative against it and zero across it.

blocks.text: The [[work|The energy a force transfers by acting over a displacement: force times displacement along the force. Met in 'When a force does work'.]] done by a force is measured in joules, and each force does its own: $+Fd$ along the displacement, $-Fd$ against it and **zero at right angles**. The *net work* is the sum of the signed works, which equals the net force times the displacement, and it is positive when the forces together add energy to the object and negative when they take it away.

recap.nextHook: Net work is what changes an object's speed, and the next lesson connects it to the energy of motion.

lessons.title: Energy of motion

lead.text: The energy an object has because it is moving is called its **kinetic energy**, and the [[work|The energy a force transfers by acting over a displacement: force times displacement along the force. Met in 'When a force does work'.]] of the last lesson shows how much it is. Start an object of mass $m$ from rest and give it a constant net force $F$ through a displacement $d$. The work done is $Fd$. By the [[second law|The acceleration of an object is the net force on it divided by its mass. Met in 'Force, mass and acceleration'.]], $F = ma$, where the acceleration is the final speed $v$ divided by the time $t$, and the displacement is the average speed $v/2$ multiplied by $t$. Putting these together, $Fd = m\,(v/t)\,(v/2)\,t$, and the time cancels.

afterFigure.text: The cancelling of the time means that the result does not depend on how long the force acted or how the speed was reached, only on the mass and the final speed. A 3 kg cart at 2 m/s has a kinetic energy of ½ × 3 × 2² = 6 J, and a 5 kg cart at 3 m/s has ½ × 5 × 3² = 22.5 J. The speed enters **squared** and the mass *only once*. Leibniz called the quantity mv² the *vis viva*, or living force, in the 1680s, and the factor of one half, which makes the energy equal to the work that creates it, was added later.

reveal.text: Doubling the speed multiplies the energy by 2² = 4, so a cart at twice the speed has four times the kinetic energy, and tripling the speed would multiply it by nine. The figure shows it for a 2 kg cart: 9 J at 3 m/s and 36 J at 6 m/s. Energy therefore grows *much faster* than speed, which is the reason that high speeds are so much more dangerous than low ones.

lead.text: The derivation of the formula started from rest, but the same argument applies to any change of speed, and it gives the **work–energy theorem**: the [[net work|The signed sum of the works of all the forces on an object. Met in 'When a force does work'.]] done on an object equals the change in its [[kinetic energy|The energy of a moving object, ½mv². Met in 'Energy of motion'.]].

afterFigure.text: A 4 kg trolley at 6 m/s has a kinetic energy of ½ × 4 × 6² = 72 J. To bring it to rest the brakes must remove all of that, so the net work is 0 − 72 = −72 J, and with a constant braking force of 18 N the stopping distance $d$ satisfies −18 × d = −72, giving 4 m. The same force on the same trolley at *twice* the speed has to remove four times the energy, and so it needs **four times the distance**, which answers the opening question.

lead.text: The [[net work|The signed sum of the works of all the forces on an object. Met in 'When a force does work'.]] is found from the kinetic energy at each end of the speeding up, and the **difference** between the two is the answer, *not* either energy alone.

workedSteps.text: The initial kinetic energy uses the initial speed.
The final kinetic energy uses the final speed, which is three times as great.
The net work is the final kinetic energy minus the initial one.

steps.headline: A 5 kg sled speeds up from 1 m/s to 3 m/s

lead.text: The same two energies are needed, and the last step is yours.

workedSteps.text: The initial kinetic energy uses the initial speed.
The final kinetic energy uses the final speed.
Both kinetic energies are now known.

reveal.text: Three times the speed means nine times the kinetic energy to remove, and the *same* braking force removes energy at the same rate per metre, so it needs nine times the distance. This is why speed limits matter so much near schools.

lessons.orientation: Use kinetic energy and net work to connect force with a change in speed.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: When a car brakes, the brakes push back against the motion over the whole stopping distance, so they do negative work, and that work has to remove whatever the moving car has that makes it hard to stop. A faster car needs more road to stop, and so does a heavier one, and what decides how much more is the way the speed and the mass each enter that amount.
The amount is the car's **kinetic energy**, the energy an object has because it is moving, and its formula follows from the work of the last lesson.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the kinetic energy of a moving object, say how it scales with mass and speed, and link net work to a change in speed.
intro.whyItMatters: Energy lets you answer questions about speed and stopping distance without following the motion second by second.

recap.keyIdea: Kinetic energy is ½mv², and the net work on an object equals the change in its kinetic energy.

blocks.text: The [[kinetic energy|The energy of a moving object, ½mv². Met in 'Energy of motion'.]] of an object is $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, so it doubles when the mass doubles and **quadruples when the speed doubles**. The [[net work|The signed sum of the works of all the forces on an object. Met in 'When a force does work'.]] on an object equals the *change* in its kinetic energy, so a constant force through a distance gives a change of speed that can be found without following the motion, and a braking force needs four times the distance to stop an object at twice the speed.

recap.nextHook: A moving object is not the only one with energy, and the next lesson counts the energy of an object that is lifted.

lessons.title: Energy and height

lead.text: When an object is lifted slowly, so that it does not speed up, the lifting force just balances its [[weight|The force of gravity on an object, W = mg, in newtons. Met in 'Weight and support'.]] $mg$, and raising it through a height $\Delta h$ takes [[work|The energy a force transfers by acting over a displacement: force times displacement along the force. Met in 'When a force does work'.]] of $mg \times \Delta h$. The energy is not lost. The object can be released and will fall and speed up, gaining as [[kinetic energy|The energy of a moving object, ½mv². Met in 'Energy of motion'.]] *exactly* the energy it was given, so the energy has been stored by the object's height, and it is called **gravitational potential energy**.

afterFigure.text: For the 6 kg bag the weight is 60 N, so a rise of 1.5 m raises the stored energy by 60 × 1.5 = 90 J, and a fall of 1.5 m changes it by 60 × (−1.5) = −90 J. Only the **change in height** enters, since the energy depends on where the object is and not on the path that took it there. "Potential" means stored and available, and the energy is a property of the object together with the Earth that pulls on it.

lead.text: Height can fall as well as rise, and then $\Delta h$ is negative, and so is $\Delta U$. A 7 kg object that descends from 3 m to 1 m has $\Delta h = 1 - 3 = -2$ m and a change of 7 × 10 × (−2) = −140 J.

On the way down gravity points along the motion, so it does positive work, and on the way up it points against it, so it does negative work. In *both* cases the work is the opposite of the energy change.

afterFigure.text: The 7 kg object that descends 2 m therefore has +140 J of work done on it by gravity, and the same energy leaves the store and appears as motion. The potential energy falls when gravity does positive work and rises when gravity does **negative work**, and the two quantities always add to zero.

lead.text: Heights have to be measured from somewhere. The potential energy at a given height depends on that choice, but nothing physical can, because only changes in potential energy ever appear in the results, and a change depends only on the *difference* of two heights.

afterFigure.text: A 2 kg object that rises from 2 m to 5 m above the floor gains 2 × 10 × 3 = 60 J. If the zero is moved to a table top 2 m above the floor, the same rise is from 0 m to 3 m, and the gain is again 2 × 10 × 3 = 60 J, because both heights have dropped by the same 2 m and the **difference is unchanged**. The potential energy at 5 m is 100 J with the floor as the zero but 60 J with the table as the zero, so it is only the gain that is the same.

Zero at a 2 m table: 0 m to 3 m

Met in 'Energy and height'.]] change comes from the [[weight|The force of gravity on an object, W = mg, in newtons. Met in 'Weight and support'.]] and the change in height, and the work of gravity follows from it.
