answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 4 m/s, half as fast

choices.label: They stop where they meet
4 m/s, half as fast
8 m/s, as fast as the first cart

questions.onCorrect: 4 m/s. The moving cart's momentum is shared by twice the mass, so the speed halves.

misconceptions.feedback: The same motion is now shared by twice the mass, so the pair cannot keep the first cart's full speed.
Nothing outside the carts pushes against the motion, so the pair keeps moving in the first cart's direction.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg cart moves at +9 m/s and hits a resting 1 kg cart. They stick together. What is their shared velocity, in m/s?
hints: Find the total momentum before.
The resting cart has no momentum.
Divide by the combined mass.
questions.onCorrect: 6 m/s. Total momentum before equals total momentum after, shared over the combined mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the moving cart's velocity. After sticking, the combined mass shares the momentum.
That is the total momentum. Divide by the combined mass.

questions.prompt: Why is the second cart's momentum negative?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.
Ask what sets the sign of momentum, given that p = mv and the mass is positive.

acceptedIdeas: It is moving in the negative direction
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is moving in the negative direction

choices.label: It is moving in the negative direction
It has less momentum than the first cart
Momentum is negative for the cart that is struck

questions.onCorrect: Momentum takes the sign of the velocity. Leftward is negative when right is positive.

misconceptions.feedback: Having less momentum than the other cart is a matter of size. The sign records direction only.
The sign comes from the direction of motion, not from which cart hits which.

questions.prompt: A 1 kg cart at 4 m/s hits an identical resting cart and they stick, moving at 2 m/s. How many joules of kinetic energy are converted to other forms?
hints: Find the kinetic energy before.
Find it again for the pair afterwards.
Subtract the energy afterwards from the energy before.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Before: ½ × 1 × 16 = 8 J. After: ½ × 2 × 4 = 4 J. Lost: 4 J.

questions.onCorrect: 4 J. Half the kinetic energy became other forms, though momentum was conserved.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the kinetic energy before. Take away what is left afterwards.
Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not in a sticking collision.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg cart at +5 m/s meets a 4 kg cart at −1 m/s. They stick. What is their shared velocity, in m/s?
hints: Give each momentum its own sign.
Add the two signed momenta.
Divide the total by the combined mass.
questions.onCorrect: +2 m/s. The negative momentum takes away from the positive one before you divide by the total mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That averages the velocities, ignoring the signs. Add the signed momenta instead.
That treats both momenta as positive and divides by one cart's mass. The second cart moves the other way, and the total is shared over both carts.

questions.prompt: A car is rolling at 10 m/s. Each second it picks up another 3 m/s. How fast is it going after 4 s, in m/s?
hints: How much does the speed gain in 4 seconds?
Four lots of 3 m/s.
Add the gain to the 10 m/s start.
questions.onCorrect: 22 m/s. A steady gain per second is the idea of acceleration: velocity changing at a steady rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gain alone, 3 m/s in each of the 4 seconds. The car was already moving at 10 m/s.
That adds only one second's gain. Count all four seconds.

questions.prompt: A cart's velocity goes from 3 m/s to 15 m/s in 4 s. What is its average acceleration in m/s²?
hints: How much did the velocity change?
Divide that change by the time it took.
Take 3 away from 15, then share it over 4 seconds.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s². Acceleration is change in velocity per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in velocity. Divide it by the time as well.
That uses the final velocity alone. Subtract the starting velocity first.

questions.prompt: Why is the acceleration positive when the cart goes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.
Work out the final velocity minus the initial velocity and look at its sign.

acceptedIdeas: Its velocity increases, from −8 up to −2.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its velocity increases, from −8 up to −2.

hints: Find the final velocity first.
Average the starting and finishing velocities.
Multiply that average by the 3 s.
questions.onCorrect: 33 m. Find the final velocity, take the mean with the start, then multiply by the time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance at the starting velocity. The cart speeds up, so it goes further.
That uses the final velocity for the whole trip. The cart was slower earlier on.

questions.prompt: A friend walks away from the door at a steady pace and is 3 m away after 2 s. How far from the door are they after 6 s, in metres?
hints: How many 2-second chunks fit into 6 seconds?
A steady pace adds the same amount to the position in every chunk.
Find what one chunk adds, then count the chunks.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 s is three lots of 2 s, so 3 × 3 = 9 m.

questions.onCorrect: 9 m. Equal times give equal steps in position, which is why a steady walk draws a straight line.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the extra time as only 3 m more. Each 2 s adds 3 m, so 6 s adds more than that.
That multiplies the distance by the time. Count how many 2 s chunks fit into 6 s.

questions.prompt: A straight position–time line passes through 4 m at 1 s and 10 m at 3 s. What is its slope in m/s?
hints: How much does the position change between the two points?
How much does the time change?
Divide the position change by the time change.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s. The slope of a position–time line is the velocity.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in position only. Divide it by the change in time.
That reads off a single point. Use the change between the two.

questions.prompt: Why does a flat stretch on this graph mean the object has stopped?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.
Ask what the vertical axis of this graph measures.

acceptedIdeas: Its position stays the same while the time goes on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its position stays the same while the time goes on

choices.label: Its position stays the same while the time goes on
The line is flat, so the velocity there is at its largest
The track is level there, so the object is not climbing

questions.onCorrect: The vertical axis is position, not height. A flat line means the position is not changing.

misconceptions.feedback: The graph does not show the track. Its vertical axis is position along the track.
The slope of a flat line is zero, and the slope is the velocity.

questions.prompt: A position–time graph has one straight segment from 20 m at 0 s to 5 m at 3 s. What velocity does it show, in m/s?
hints: Is the position rising or falling?
Final position minus initial position, over the time.
Take 20 away from 5, then share it over the 3 s.
questions.onCorrect: −5 m/s. The line falls, so the velocity is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the position falls. Show that with a sign.
That is the change in position. Divide it by the time as well.

questions.prompt: Cycling at a steady pace, you cover 20 m in 4 s. How many metres do you cover each second?
hints: Share the 20 m equally across the 4 seconds.
Each second covers the same distance.
How many 4s fit into 20?
questions.onCorrect: 5 m/s. Sharing a distance equally over the time taken is the idea behind every speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the two numbers. Each second covers less than the whole 20 m, so divide.

questions.prompt: A cart's displacement is −10 m over 5 s. What is its average velocity in m/s?
hints: Which quantity is on the top of the division: distance or displacement?
Divide the signed displacement by the elapsed time.
Keep the minus sign through the division.
questions.onCorrect: −2 m/s. Dividing by a positive time keeps the sign of the displacement.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but velocity carries the direction. The displacement was negative.
That multiplies by the time. Divide the displacement by it.

questions.prompt: Why are the two averages different for this trip?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.
Ask which quantity each average divides by the elapsed time.

acceptedIdeas: The turn makes the displacement smaller than the distance
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The turn makes the displacement smaller than the distance

choices.label: Velocity counts only the first stretch of the trip, before the turn
The turn makes the displacement smaller than the distance
The two averages are divided by different elapsed times

questions.onCorrect: Turning back shrinks the displacement but not the distance, while the elapsed time is the same for both.

misconceptions.feedback: Velocity uses both stretches: line 4 took the westward stretch away from the eastward one. Look at the quantity that is divided by the elapsed time.
Both averages use the same elapsed time, 8 s. Look at the quantity divided by it.

questions.prompt: A walker goes 30 m east in 5 s, then 6 m west in 1 s. With east positive, what is the average velocity over the whole trip, in m/s?
hints: Subtract the westward distance from the eastward distance to get the net move.
Add the two times to get the whole trip's time.
Divide the net move by the total time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Displacement 30 − 6 = +24 m over 6 s gives +4 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: +4 m/s. Net displacement over total time: the westward stretch partly cancels the eastward one.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the whole path length by the time. That is the average speed, not the velocity.
The walker finishes east of the start, so the net movement is eastward.

questions.prompt: What force does gravity exert on a 6 kg bag, in newtons? Take g = 10 N per kilogram.
hints: How much pull is there on one kilogram?
Each kilogram has its own 10 N.
Count the kilograms and multiply.
questions.onCorrect: 60 N. The pull on each kilogram times the number of kilograms: mg.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. Each kilogram gets its own 10 N, so multiply.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object weighs 30 N on Earth. On a planet where g = 4 m/s², what does it weigh, in newtons?
hints: Does the 3 kg change when the object moves?
Weight is mass times g for the new planet.
Multiply the mass by the new g.
questions.onCorrect: 12 N. The mass is still 3 kg. Only g changed, so the weight did.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the weight on Earth. The new planet has a different g.
That adds the mass and g. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A 7 kg box rests on a shelf. Only its weight and the shelf's upward force act, with g = 10 m/s². What is the upward force from the shelf, in newtons?
hints: Is the box accelerating?
Then the net force is zero.
The shelf force must match the weight.
questions.onCorrect: 70 N. With no acceleration, the support force equals the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: The box is not falling, so something is holding it up.
That is the mass. The force is mass times g.

questions.prompt: Why must the support force be larger than the weight here?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.
Write the net force as support minus weight, and ask what sign it needs for an upward acceleration.

acceptedIdeas: An upward acceleration needs a net force that points up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An upward acceleration needs a net force that points up

choices.label: An upward acceleration needs a net force that points up
The object's weight increases while the lift is moving
Gravity pulls less on the object while the lift rises

questions.onCorrect: Net force is support minus weight. For an upward acceleration it has to be positive.

misconceptions.feedback: The weight stays mg. It is the support that changes.
Gravity keeps pulling with the same weight. The support has to do more than balance it.

questions.prompt: A 6 kg load in a lift accelerates downward at 3 m/s². Only its weight and the support force act, with g = 10 m/s². What is the support force, in newtons?
hints: Upward is positive, so the acceleration is negative.
Use support force = m(g + a) with a negative.
Take the acceleration off g, then multiply by the mass.
questions.onCorrect: 42 N. The load accelerates down, so the support force is less than the weight.

misconceptions.feedback: That only balances the weight. The load is accelerating downward, so the support gives less than that.
That treats the acceleration as upward. It points down, so it reduces the support force.

questions.prompt: A steady push moves a box 2 m and costs 20 units of effort. The same push moves the box 8 m. How many units of effort does that cost?
hints: How much effort is each metre?
The push is the same, so each metre costs the same.
Multiply the cost per metre by 8.
questions.onCorrect: 80 units. Same push, four times the distance, four times the effort. Physics calls this effort work.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the extra distance to the cost. The cost grows in step with the distance.

questions.prompt: A constant 9 N force acts along a 6 m displacement. How much work does it do, in joules?
hints: Do the force and the displacement point the same way?
Then the work is positive.
Multiply the force by the distance.
questions.onCorrect: 54 J. Work is force times displacement along the force. The joule is one newton times one metre.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two numbers. Multiply them.
That divides force by distance. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: Why is the work done by friction negative?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.
Ask which way friction points compared with the way the crate moves.

acceptedIdeas: Friction points against the displacement
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Friction points against the displacement

choices.label: The crate is slowing down while friction acts
Friction is smaller than the push
Friction points against the displacement

questions.onCorrect: A force against the displacement does negative work, whatever its size.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not decide the sign. Direction relative to the movement does.
The crate is pulled with the larger force, so it speeds up. The sign of friction's work comes from its direction and not from whether the crate slows.

questions.prompt: A 12 N pull acts along a 5 m displacement while 9 N of friction acts against it. What is the net work, in joules?
hints: Find the work of each force with its sign.
Friction's work is negative.
Add the two signed works.
questions.onCorrect: +15 J. Add each force's signed work. Friction takes away from the pull's work.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two works as if both were positive. Friction's work is negative.
That is the net force alone. Multiply by the distance to get work.

questions.prompt: One student reads a trip as 2 m to 9 m. A second student's zero sits 10 m behind the first student's, so she reads 12 m to 19 m. What displacement does the second student find, in metres?
hints: What are the second student's starting and finishing readings?
Displacement is the finishing reading minus the starting one.
Take 12 away from 19.
questions.onCorrect: +7 m. Moving the origin adds the same amount to both readings, so the displacement does not change.

misconceptions.feedback: 10 m is the gap between the two zeros. The trolley's move is the gap between its own two readings.
That is the finishing reading on its own. Take the starting reading away from it.

questions.prompt: A cart starts from rest with constant acceleration and covers 6 m in its first 2 s. How far has it gone after 4 s, in metres?
hints: Does the cart go as far in its second 2 s as in its first?
From rest, the displacement depends on the square of the time.
Doubling the time multiplies the distance by 2².

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From rest the displacement is ½at². Doubling t multiplies it by 2² = 4, so 6 × 4 = 24 m. (Here a = 3 m/s²: ½ × 3 × 4² = 24 m.)

questions.onCorrect: 24 m. From rest, distance grows with the square of the time, so twice the time gives four times the distance.

misconceptions.feedback: Doubling the time doubles the distance only at a steady velocity. This cart speeds up, so the second 2 s cover more ground than the first.
That is how far the cart goes in the second 2 s alone. The question asks for the distance from the start, which includes the first 2 s.

questions.prompt: What is the average speed for the whole trip, in m/s?
hints: How much ground does the whole trip cover?
How long does the whole trip take, with both stretches together?
Divide the total ground by the total time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The trip is 12 + 12 = 24 m in 2 + 6 = 8 s, so the average speed is 24 ÷ 8 = 3 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s. Add the distances, add the times, then divide once: 24 m over 8 s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean of the two stretch speeds. The slow stretch lasts three times as long, so it counts for more.
That divides the time by the distance. Speed is distance per second.

questions.prompt: A runner stops exactly on the line where she started. How far is she from where she began, in metres?
hints: Where is she compared with the start line?
She has finished on the line she began from.
How far apart are a place and itself?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: She finishes on the line she started from, so the two places are 0 m apart.

questions.onCorrect: 0 m. The 400 m she ran says how much ground she covered, but it says nothing about how far apart her start and finish are.

misconceptions.feedback: The length of the lap is how much ground she covered. This question asks how far her finishing place is from her starting place.

questions.prompt: On a straight track the origin is at the door and the positive direction points to the right. A trolley sits 3 m to the left of the door. What is its position, in metres?
hints: Which side of the origin is the trolley on?
The left is the side opposite the positive direction.
Give the size, 3, with the sign for that side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The trolley is 3 m from the origin on the side opposite the positive direction, so its position is −3 m.

questions.onCorrect: −3 m. The size is the number of metres from the origin, and the minus sign says it lies on the side opposite the positive direction.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the trolley is on the side opposite the positive direction, and the sign has to show that.
Zero is the position of the origin itself, which is the door. The trolley is 3 m from it.

questions.prompt: Usain Bolt ran 100 m in 9.58 s. Divide the distance by the time: how many metres per second is that, to the nearest tenth?
hints: Divide the distance by the time.
Divide 100 by 9.58.
Round the result to one decimal place.
questions.onCorrect: 10.4 m/s. He did not run at this rate throughout: it is the figure for the whole race, with a slower start and a faster middle.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the time by the distance. The quantity wanted is the metres covered in each second.
That multiplies the two numbers. The distance has to be shared out over the seconds, so divide.

questions.prompt: A swimmer swims 50 m along a pool and 50 m back in 80 s. What is her average speed, in m/s?
hints: How much ground does she cover in total?
Count the length there and the length back.
Divide the total distance by 80 s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The distance is 50 + 50 = 100 m, so the average speed is 100 ÷ 80 = 1.25 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: 1.25 m/s. Speed counts the whole 100 m of the swim, although she finishes where she began.

misconceptions.feedback: That is her average velocity, which is zero because she finishes where she began. Speed uses the distance she swam.
That counts only one length of the pool. She swims there and back.

questions.prompt: A trolley's position is 0 m at 0 s and 6 m at 3 s, stays at 6 m until 5 s, and is 12 m at 8 s. What is its average velocity over the whole 8 s, in m/s?
hints: Use the first point and the last point.
The elapsed time runs from 0 s to 8 s, rest included.
Divide the change in position by 8 s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The displacement is 12 − 0 = 12 m over 8 s, so the average velocity is 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 m/s.

questions.onCorrect: +1.5 m/s. The rest counts as time, so the 8 s are divided into the 12 m.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the 2 s at rest. The elapsed time on the graph runs from the first point to the last.
That is the change in position on its own. Divide it by the elapsed time as well.

questions.prompt: What is the average acceleration, in m/s²?
hints: The change in velocity is final minus initial.
The velocity falls, so the change is negative.
Divide the change by 4 s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The change is 4 − 20 = −16 m/s, and −16 ÷ 4 = −4 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: −4 m/s². The velocity falls by 4 m/s every second, so the acceleration is negative.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the velocity falls. The sign has to show that.
That is the change in velocity. Divide it by the time as well.

questions.prompt: With upward positive, a ball leaves a hand at 12 m/s, and 2 s later it is moving downward at 8 m/s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: A downward velocity is negative when upward is positive.
Final velocity minus initial velocity.
Divide the change by the 2 s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The change is −8 − 12 = −20 m/s, and −20 ÷ 2 = −10 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: −10 m/s². The velocity falls by 10 m/s every second, whether the ball is rising or falling.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads the final velocity as +8 m/s. The ball is moving down, so its velocity is negative.
The size is right, but the velocity changes towards the negative direction. The sign has to show that.

questions.prompt: What is the ball's height above the start after 3 s, in metres?
hints: Find the distance the initial velocity alone would give in 3 s.
Find the distance gravity takes back in 3 s.
Subtract the second from the first.
questions.onCorrect: 30 m. The ball passed its top at 2.5 s and is coming down, but it is still 30 m above where it started.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores gravity. The ball slows as it rises and then falls back, so it is far lower than that.
That is only the distance gravity takes back. Add the distance from the initial velocity as well.

questions.prompt: With upward positive and g = 10 m/s², a stone is thrown straight down at 5 m/s. Find its velocity after 2 s, in m/s.
hints: A downward velocity is negative when upward is positive.
Gravity adds to a downward velocity, so it adds a negative amount.
Calculate −5 + (−10) × 2.
questions.onCorrect: −25 m/s. The stone starts at 5 m/s downward and gains another 10 m/s downward each second.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes gravity as adding upward velocity. Gravity points down, so it adds to the downward velocity.
That leaves out the 5 m/s the stone started with. Include the initial velocity.
The size is right, but the stone moves down. With upward positive, its velocity is negative.

questions.prompt: How big is the leftward force, in newtons?
hints: What does a steady velocity say about the net force?
The leftward force has to cancel all the rightward force.
Add the two rightward forces.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The net force is zero, so the leftward force equals 15 + 9 = 24 N.

questions.onCorrect: 24 N. A steady velocity means zero net force, so the leftward force matches the total rightward force.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the difference of the two rightward forces. Both of them need cancelling, so add them.
With no leftward force the crate would speed up. A steady velocity needs the forces to cancel.

questions.prompt: A lamp hangs motionless from a cable that pulls upward on it with 30 N. Only the cable and gravity act on the lamp. How big is the pull of gravity on it, in newtons?
hints: A lamp at rest has a velocity that is not changing.
What does that say about the net force?
The two forces must cancel.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lamp is at rest, so the net force is zero and the pull of gravity equals the cable's 30 N.

questions.onCorrect: 30 N. The lamp is at rest, so the two vertical forces balance each other exactly.

misconceptions.feedback: Gravity acts on every object near the Earth. The lamp stays still because the cable's pull cancels it.
That adds the two forces. They point in opposite directions and have to cancel.

questions.prompt: A 1200 kg car is speeding up at 2.5 m/s². What net force acts on it, in newtons?
hints: This time the mass and the acceleration are known.
Multiply them to find the net force.
Calculate 1200 × 2.5.
questions.onCorrect: 3000 N. The net force is the mass multiplied by the acceleration, however large the object.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the mass by the acceleration. To find a force, multiply the mass by the acceleration.
That adds the two numbers. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg bag rests on a table on the Moon, where g = 1.6 m/s². What is the table's upward force on the bag, in newtons?
hints: Is the bag accelerating?
Then the support force equals the weight.
Multiply the mass by the Moon's g.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The support force equals the weight: 4 × 1.6 = 6.4 N.

questions.onCorrect: 6.4 N. At rest the support force still equals the weight, and the weight depends on the Moon's smaller g.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force the table would need to give on Earth. The Moon's g is smaller.
That subtracts g from the mass. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: On smooth ice a 50 kg skater pushes a 100 kg skater with a force of 60 N. The push is the only horizontal force on the 100 kg skater. Find that skater's acceleration in m/s².
hints: Use the force on the 100 kg skater and that skater's own mass.
The 50 kg skater's mass does not enter this calculation.
Calculate 60 ÷ 100.
questions.onCorrect: 0.6 m/s². Use the force on the skater and that skater's own mass.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the mass of the skater who is pushing. Use the mass of the skater being pushed.
That multiplies force by mass. Divide the force by the mass.

questions.prompt: What is the box's acceleration, in m/s², with right positive?
hints: Sliding friction is the only horizontal force.
It points against the sliding, so it is negative.
Divide the force by 5 kg.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The friction is 0.3 × 5 × 10 = 15 N to the left, so a = −15 ÷ 5 = −3 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: −3 m/s². Friction is the only horizontal force, and it points against the sliding, so the box slows.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but friction points against the sliding. With right positive the acceleration is negative.
Without a push, friction is the only horizontal force on the box, so the net force is not zero.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box rests on a floor with μ_s = 0.5. A second identical 4 kg box is placed on top of it. With g = 10 m/s², what is the maximum static friction on the lower box, in newtons?
hints: The floor supports both boxes.
The support force is the weight of the two boxes together.
Multiply that by 0.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The support force is 8 × 10 = 80 N, so f_s,max = 0.5 × 80 = 40 N.

questions.onCorrect: 40 N. The support force on the lower box doubles, so the limit doubles, and the coefficient is unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the lower box. The floor supports both boxes.
That is the support force. Multiply it by the coefficient as well.

questions.prompt: What is the net work, in joules?
hints: Find the work of each force with its sign.
The friction's work is negative.
Add the two signed works.
questions.onCorrect: +24 J. The push adds 36 J and the friction takes away 12 J.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two works as if both were positive. Friction's work is negative.
That is the net force alone. Multiply by the distance to get work.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg stone falls 5 m. The pull of gravity on it is 20 N and acts along the fall. How much work does gravity do on the stone, in joules?
hints: Gravity acts in the direction the stone moves.
Multiply the force by the distance of the fall.
Calculate 20 × 5.
questions.onCorrect: +100 J. Gravity points along the fall, so its work is positive: the force times the distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the force by the mass. The work is the force times the distance of the fall.
That multiplies the mass by the distance. Use the force of 20 N.

questions.prompt: What net work is done on the sled, in joules?
hints: Find the kinetic energy at the start and at the end.
Net work is the final energy minus the initial energy.
Calculate 22.5 − 2.5.
questions.onCorrect: 20 J. Net work equals the change in kinetic energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the final kinetic energy alone. Net work is the change: final minus initial.
That uses the change in speed with the mass. Work is the change in ½mv².

questions.prompt: A car's brakes stop it from 10 m/s in 20 m. With the same braking force, how far does the car travel before stopping from 30 m/s? Give the distance in metres.
hints: How many times greater is the speed?
The kinetic energy to remove grows with the square of the speed.
Multiply the 20 m by that factor.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three times the speed means 3² = 9 times the kinetic energy, so 9 × 20 = 180 m.

questions.onCorrect: 180 m. The distance grows with the square of the speed when the braking force is the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That triples the distance with the speed. The energy to remove grows with the square of the speed.
That squares the original distance. The factor is the square of the speed ratio, which is 3.

questions.prompt: What is its gravitational potential-energy change, in joules?
hints: Find the weight of the object first.
The change in height is the final height minus the initial height.
Multiply the weight by the change in height.
questions.onCorrect: 150 J. The weight of 50 N is multiplied by the 3 m rise.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the final height instead of the change in height.
That leaves out g. Multiply the weight by the change in height.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg object is 3 m above the floor. Taking the top of a table 1 m above the floor as the zero of height, and g = 10 m/s², what is the object's gravitational potential energy, in joules?
hints: How high is the object above the table top?
The table top is the zero, so subtract its height from the object's height.
Multiply the weight by that height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The object is 3 − 1 = 2 m above the table top, so U = 4 × 10 × 2 = 80 J.

questions.onCorrect: 80 J. With the table top as the zero, only the height above the table counts.

misconceptions.feedback: That measures the height from the floor. The table top is the zero here.
That uses the table's height as the object's height. Use the object's height above the table.

questions.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest through 45 m. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², what is its speed on reaching the ground, in m/s?
hints: The potential energy lost becomes kinetic energy, and the mass cancels.
Use v² = 2gh.
Take the square root of 2 × 10 × 45.
questions.onCorrect: 30 m/s. The mass cancels, so the speed after a drop depends on the height and g alone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed squared. Take the square root to find the speed.
That is gh. Double it and take the square root.

questions.prompt: What is its kinetic energy at the bottom, in joules?
hints: Find the potential energy released by the drop.
Take the heating off that amount.
Calculate 120 − 45.
questions.onCorrect: 75 J. Potential energy released, minus the heating, leaves the kinetic energy.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the heating. Some of the released energy went into thermal energy.
That adds the heating. Heating takes energy away from the motion.

questions.prompt: A 2 kg ball is thrown straight up at 10 m/s. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how high above the throwing point does it rise, in metres?
hints: Find the ball's kinetic energy at the start.
At the top it is momentarily at rest, so all of that energy is potential.
Set mgh equal to that kinetic energy.
questions.onCorrect: 5 m. The kinetic energy at the start pays for the potential energy at the top.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy, not the height. Set mgh equal to it and solve for h.
That is the speed. Equate the starting kinetic energy with mgh to find the height.

questions.prompt: What input power does it need, in watts?
hints: Efficiency is useful power out divided by power in.
Rearrange to input = output ÷ efficiency.
Divide 60 by 0.25.
questions.onCorrect: 240 W. The input power is the useful output power divided by the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the output by the efficiency. The input is the larger number, so divide.
That adds the efficiency as if it were 25 W. Use the fraction 0.25.

questions.prompt: A motor raises a 20 kg load through 4 m in 5 s. With g = 10 m/s², and counting only the energy that the load gains, what useful power does the motor deliver, in watts?
hints: Find the potential energy the load gains.
That is the useful energy delivered.
Divide it by the 5 s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The load gains 20 × 10 × 4 = 800 J in 5 s, so P = 800 ÷ 5 = 160 W.

questions.onCorrect: 160 W. The energy gained by the load, 800 J, divided by the time it took.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the energy gained. Divide it by the time to get a power.
That is the weight of the load. Find the energy first, then divide by the time.

questions.prompt: What is its final velocity, in m/s?
hints: Find the initial momentum, which is negative.
Add the impulse with its sign.
Divide the final momentum by the mass.
questions.onCorrect: +2 m/s. The impulse is larger than the momentum the cart began with, so the cart ends up moving the other way.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the impulse by the mass and adds nothing for the starting velocity. Start from the initial momentum.
That subtracts the impulse. A positive impulse adds to the momentum.

questions.prompt: A 0.3 kg ball moving right at 10 m/s is caught and brought to rest in 0.05 s. With right positive, what is the average net force on it, in newtons?
hints: Find the change in momentum: final minus initial.
The ball ends at rest.
Divide the change by 0.05 s.
questions.onCorrect: −60 N. The force points against the ball's motion, and it is large because the stop is so quick.

questions.prompt: What is their shared final velocity, in m/s?

questions.prompt: A 1 kg cart at +10 m/s hits a resting 9 kg cart and they stick. External impulse is negligible. Find their shared final velocity in m/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first cart's velocity. After sticking, the combined mass shares the momentum.

questions.prompt: A cart is moving to the left with a velocity of −3 m/s, and its acceleration is +2 m/s². What happens to its speed while those signs remain?

questions.prompt: A lamp hangs motionless from two cables that pull upward on it with 11 N and 14 N. Only the cables and gravity act on the lamp. How big is the pull of gravity on it, in newtons?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lamp is at rest, so the net force is zero and the pull of gravity equals the two upward pulls together: 11 + 14 = 25 N.

questions.prompt: A block moves right at a constant velocity. Ropes pull it right with 35 N and 25 N, and a third rope pulls it left with 40 N. Friction also acts on the block. How big is the friction, in newtons?
hints: What does constant velocity say about the net force?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Constant velocity means zero net force. The rightward forces total 35 + 25 = 60 N, so the leftward forces must also total 60 N. The rope gives 40 N of that, so the friction is 20 N.

questions.onCorrect: 20 N. The rightward forces total 60 N, so the leftward forces must total 60 N too, and the rope supplies 40 N of that.

misconceptions.feedback: With no friction the block would speed up to the right. A steady velocity needs the forces to cancel.

questions.prompt: Cart A and cart B push each other with 10 N. A student also pushes cart A to the right with 6 N, and nothing else pushes either cart horizontally. With right positive, what is the net horizontal force on the two carts taken together, in newtons?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The forces between the carts are +10 N on B and −10 N on A, and they sum to 0 N. Only the student's +6 N comes from outside the pair, so the net force on the pair is +6 N.

questions.prompt: A heavy crate on a level floor does not move when you push it horizontally with 30 N. You push harder, with 45 N, and it still does not move. By how many newtons has the friction on the crate grown?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The crate is at rest both times, so friction equals the push each time: 30 N, then 45 N. It has grown by 45 − 30 = 15 N.

questions.onCorrect: 15 N. Friction matched each push exactly, so it grew by as much as the push did. It adjusts to what it has to cancel.

misconceptions.feedback: Each of those is the friction at one of the pushes. The question asks how much it has grown from the first to the second.

questions.prompt: A 4 kg box rests on a floor. A horizontal push of 12 N does not move it. A second person then adds a 5 N push in the same direction, and the box still does not move. How big is the static friction on it now, in newtons?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The box stays at rest, so static friction matches the total push: 12 + 5 = 17 N.

questions.prompt: A constant 30 N push acts due north on a cart that rolls 4 m due east. Find the work done by this push on the cart, in joules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The push is at right angles to the displacement, so none of it acts along the motion and its work is 0 J.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the force by the distance. The push is at right angles to the motion, so none of it acts along it.

questions.prompt: A 3 kg object rises from 2 m to 5 m above the floor, with g = 10 m/s². The zero of height is then moved from the floor to a table top 1 m above the floor. What is the object's gravitational potential-energy change with the table top as the zero, in joules?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: With the table top as the zero the heights are 1 m and 4 m, so ΔU = 3 × 10 × (4 − 1) = 90 J, the same as with the floor as the zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the potential energy the ball still has after 2 m. The kinetic energy is the energy it has lost.
